item.title: Annotate Command (annotate)
item.description:
Annotations included with the backup command can be added, modified, or removed afterwards using the annotate command.

Command Options

Backup Annotation Option (--annotation)

Annotate backup with user-defined key/value pairs.

Users can attach informative key/value pairs to the backup. This option may be used multiple times to attach multiple annotations.

Annotations are output by the info command text output when a backup is specified with --set and always appear in the JSON output.

item.title: Cluster / Instance
item.description:
Select instance and cluster types that meet your requirements.

Pigsty supports several PostgreSQL instance and cluster types:

  • Primary: Define a single instance cluster.
  • Replica: Define a basic HA cluster with one primary and one replica.
  • Offline: Define an instance dedicated to OLAP/ETL/interactive queries
  • Sync Standby: Enable synchronous commit to ensure no data loss.
  • Quorum Commit: Use quorum sync commit for a higher consistency level.
  • Standby Cluster: Clone an existing cluster and follow it
  • Delayed Cluster: Clone an existing cluster for emergency data recovery
  • Citus Cluster: Define a Citus distributed database cluster

Primary

The simplest cluster contains one primary instance:

item.description:
Quick Reference

Clone Cluster - Clone via standby cluster or PITR

For other management tasks, see: HA Management, Manage Users, Manage Databases.

item.title: Dynamic Configuration Settings
item.description:
Dynamic configuration is stored in the DCS (Distributed Configuration Store) and applied on all cluster nodes.

In order to change the dynamic configuration you can use either patronictl_edit_config tool or Patroni REST API.

  • loop_wait: the number of seconds the loop will sleep. Default value: 10, minimum possible value: 1
  • ttl: the TTL to acquire the leader lock (in seconds). Think of it as the length of time before initiation of the automatic failover process. Default value: 30, minimum possible value: 20
  • retry_timeout: timeout for DCS and PostgreSQL operation retries (in seconds). DCS or network issues shorter than this will not cause Patroni to demote the leader. Default value: 10, minimum possible value: 3
Warning

when changing values of loop_wait, retry_timeout, or ttl you have to follow the rule:

loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout <= ttl

item.title: Features
item.description:
“PostgreSQL In Great STYle”: Postgres, Infras, Graphics, Service, Toolbox, it’s all Yours.

—— Battery-included, local-first PostgreSQL distribution, open-source RDS alternative

Value Propositions

  • Extensibility: Powerful extensions out of the box: deep integration of PostGIS, TimescaleDB, Citus, PGVector, 600 plugins, and 12 PG kernels.
  • Reliability: Quickly create high-availability, self-healing PostgreSQL clusters with built-in point-in-time recovery, access control, a self-signed CA, and TLS.
  • Observability: Prometheus and Grafana provide a modular monitoring stack that can operate independently. See the Gallery and Demo.
  • Availability: Deliver stable, reliable, auto-routed, transaction-pooled, read-write separated high-performance database services, with flexible access modes via HAProxy, Pgbouncer, and VIP.
  • Maintainability: Easy to use, Infrastructure as Code, Management SOPs, auto-tuning, local software repository, Vagrant sandbox and OpenTofu templates, zero-downtime migration solutions.
  • Composability: Modular architecture design, reusable Infra, various optional modules: Redis, Silo object storage, ETCD, DuckDB, Docker, Supabase.

Overview

Pigsty is a local, open-source alternative to PostgreSQL RDS:

item.title: Features
item.description:
• Several levels of brutality when rotating connections:

    Session pooling
    Most polite method. When a client connects, a server connection will be assigned to it for the whole duration it stays connected. When the client disconnects, the server connection will be put back into pool. This mode supports all PostgreSQL features.
    Transaction pooling
    A server connection is assigned to a client only during a transaction. When PgBouncer notices that the transaction is over, the server will be put back into the pool. This mode breaks a few session-based features of PostgreSQL. You can use it only when the application cooperates by not using features that break. See the table below for incompatible features.
    Statement pooling
    Most aggressive method. This is transaction pooling with a twist: Multi-statement transactions are disallowed. This is meant to enforce “autocommit” mode on the client, mostly targeted at PL/Proxy.

  • Low memory requirements (2 kB per connection by default). This is because PgBouncer does not need to see full packets at once.

  • It is not tied to one backend server. The destination databases can reside on different hosts.

  • Supports online reconfiguration for most settings.

  • Supports rolling restarts and upgrades using multiple processes with so_reuseport. The legacy online restart (-R) was removed in 1.26.0.

item.title: Getting Started
item.description:
This tutorial installs PostgreSQL 18 and pgvector, starts a local test instance, and enables the extension in a database.

Use a supported Linux test host with internet access and curl installed. You need root or sudo access. Run the commands in order.

Install PIG 

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/pig | bash
pig version

In mainland China, use https://repo.pigsty.cc/pig instead. The installer selects the RPM or DEB package for your host. See Installation for other methods.

item.title: E-R Model of Infra Cluster
item.description:
The INFRA module is a management hub made of infrastructure nodes, rather than a traditional cluster. It provides core services for the deployment. Each node is an autonomous service unit that runs components such as Nginx, Grafana, and VictoriaMetrics. Together, these nodes provide observability and management for database clusters.

There are two core entities in Pigsty’s INFRA module:

  • Node: A server that runs infrastructure components. It can be a physical server, VM, container, or Pod.
  • Component: An infrastructure service on a node, such as Nginx, Grafana, or VictoriaMetrics.

INFRA nodes usually also serve as administration nodes, which form the Pigsty control plane.

item.title: Introduction
item.description:
Patroni is a template for high availability (HA) PostgreSQL solutions using Python. Patroni originated as a fork of Governor, the project from Compose. It includes plenty of new features.

For additional background info, see:

  • PostgreSQL HA with Kubernetes and Patroni, talk by Josh Berkus at KubeCon 2016 (video)
  • Feb. 2016 Zalando Tech blog post

Development Status

Patroni is in active development and accepts contributions. See our Contributing section below for more details.

item.title: News
item.description:
pgBackRest 2.60.0 Released

October 18, 2026

The pgBackRest community is pleased to announce the release of pgBackRest 2.60.0, the latest version of the reliable, easy-to-use backup and restore solution that can seamlessly scale up to the largest databases and workloads.

pgBackRest supports a robust set of features for managing your backup and recovery infrastructure, including: parallel backup/restore, full/differential/incremental backups, block incremental backup, multiple repositories, delta restore, parallel asynchronous archiving, malware/ransomware protection, per-file checksums, page checksums (when enabled) validated during backup, multiple compression types, encryption, partial/failed backup resume, backup from standby, tablespace and link support, S3/Azure/GCS/SFTP support, backup expiration, local/remote operation via SSH or TLS, flexible configuration, and more.

item.title: Parameter Optimization Policy
item.description:
Pigsty provides four parameter templates for different workloads. Select a template with pg_conf.

  • tiny.yml: Optimized for small nodes, VMs, and demos (the template is labeled for 1-3 cores)
  • oltp.yml: Optimized for OLTP workloads and latency-sensitive applications (4C8GB+) (default template)
  • olap.yml: Optimized for OLAP workloads and throughput (4C8G+)
  • crit.yml: Optimized for data consistency and critical applications (4C8G+)

The following sections describe the optimization settings for these four templates.

Memory Parameter Tuning

Pigsty detects the system’s memory size. It uses this value to set the maximum number of connections and memory-related parameters.

item.title: RPO Trade-offs
item.description:
RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines the maximum amount of data loss allowed when the primary fails.

Critical data, such as financial transactions, typically requires RPO = 0: no data loss.

Stricter RPO targets increase write latency and reduce throughput. Replica failure can also make the primary unavailable. Some workloads accept limited data loss for higher performance and availability.

Trade-offs

Asynchronous replicas normally lag behind the primary by about 10KB–100KB or 100µs–10ms, depending on network and throughput. At primary failure, a replica might not have received the latest data. Promotion can lose those unreplicated changes.

item.title: YAML Configuration Settings
item.description:
Global/Universal

  • thread_pool_size: size of thread pool used by Patroni to execute asynchronous tasks and communicate via REST API with other members during leader race or failsafe checks. Minimal value is 5, default value is 5.
  • thread_stack_size: specifies the stack size to be used for threads started by Patroni. Value must be aligned by 64kB. Minimal value is 64kB, default value (set by Patroni) is 512kB.
  • name: the name of the host. Must be unique for the cluster.
  • namespace: path within the configuration store where Patroni will keep information about the cluster. Default value: “/service”
  • scope: cluster name

item.title: Archive Get Command (archive-get)
item.description:
This command is used by PostgreSQL to restore a backup, perform PITR, or as an alternative to streaming for keeping a replica up to date. WAL segments are required for PostgreSQL recovery or to maintain a replica.

When multiple repositories are configured, WAL will be fetched from the repositories in priority order (e.g. repo1, repo2, etc.). In general it is better if faster/cheaper storage has higher priority. If a repository is specified with the --repo option then only that repository will be searched.

item.title: Configuration: pgbouncer.ini
item.description:
Description

The configuration file is in “ini” format. Section names are between [ and ]. Lines starting with ; or # are taken as comments and ignored. The characters ; and # are not recognized as special when they appear later in the line.

Generic settings

logfile

Specifies the log file. For daemonization (-d), either this or syslog needs to be set.

Failure Model

Item Best Worst Average Description
Crash Found 0 loop loop/2 Best: PG crashes right before check
Worst: PG crashes right after check
Restart Timeout 0 start start Best: PG recovers instantly
Worst: Wait full start timeout before releasing lease
Replica Detect 0 loop loop/2 Best: Right at check point
Worst: Just missed check point
Elect Promote 0 2 1 Best: Acquire lock and promote directly
Worst: API timeout + Promote
HAProxy Check (rise-1) × fastinter (rise-1) × fastinter + inter (rise-1) × fastinter + inter/2 Best: State changes before check
Worst: State changes right after check

item.title: History
item.description:
Historical Origins

Pigsty began in 2018-2019 at Tantan. Tantan is a dating app similar to Tinder in China, later acquired by Momo. Its founding engineering team was Swedish, and its startup culture followed a Nordic model.

Tantan used PostgreSQL and Go as its core stack. Its architecture followed Instagram and centered on PostgreSQL. It served several million daily active users, millions of TPS, and hundreds of TB of data. The data layer used only PostgreSQL. PG stored procedures implemented almost all business logic, including 100ms recommendation algorithms. This was arguably one of China’s most complex large-scale PostgreSQL deployments at the time.

item.title: Installation
item.description:
Pre-requirements for Mac OS

To install requirements on a Mac, run the following:

brew install postgresql etcd haproxy libyaml python

Psycopg

Starting from psycopg2-2.8 the binary version of psycopg2 will no longer be installed by default. Installing it from the source code requires C compiler and postgres+python dev packages. Since in the python world it is not possible to specify dependency as psycopg2 OR psycopg2-binary you will have to decide how to install it.

item.title: Introduction
item.description:
PIG is a command-line tool for installing and managing PostgreSQL and its extensions. It maps extension names to RPM or DEB packages and uses apt, dnf, or yum to install them.

The catalog contains 616 extension entries. PIG selects package names for your PostgreSQL major version, operating system, and CPU architecture. It also provides commands for source builds, local PostgreSQL operations, backups, and Pigsty administration.

What you can do

Task Command Reference
Find an extension and check package availability pig ext list, pig ext avail Extensions
Add PGDG and Pigsty repositories pig repo add pgsql -u Repositories
Install PostgreSQL 18 and pgvector pig install -v 18 pg18 vector Getting started
Build an extension package from source pig build pkg NAME Build
Start, inspect, or stop a local PostgreSQL instance pig pg PostgreSQL
Manage a Patroni cluster pig pt Patroni
Back up or restore an instance pig pb, pig pitr pgBackRest, PITR
Configure Pigsty and run its playbooks pig sty, pig inventory, pig do Pigsty

Start with the tutorial to install PostgreSQL and enable your first extension.

item.title: Kernel Version
item.description:
Choosing a “kernel” in Pigsty means determining the PostgreSQL major version, mode/distribution, packages to install, and tuning templates to load.

The Pigsty v4.5 source supports PostgreSQL 14-18 and uses 18 by default. Use the following configuration settings to select a kernel.

Major Version and Packages

  • pg_version: Select the PostgreSQL major version. The default is 18. Pigsty maps the version to the correct package name prefix.
  • pg_packages: Select core packages with package aliases. The default, pgsql-main pgsql-common, includes the kernel, Patroni, PgBouncer, pgBackRest, and other common tools.
  • pg_extensions: Select additional extension packages. Aliases are supported. The default is empty, which installs only core dependencies.
all:
 vars:
 pg_version: 18
 pg_packages: [ pgsql-main, pgsql-common ]
 pg_extensions: [ postgis, timescaledb, pgvector, pgml ]

During installation, Ansible downloads packages for pg_version=18 and installs extension files on the system. Database initialization scripts can then run CREATE EXTENSION.

item.title: OLTP Template
item.description:
oltp.yml is Pigsty’s default configuration template for online transaction processing (OLTP). It is designed for CPUs with 4-128 cores and provides high concurrency, low latency, and high throughput.

Pair with node_tune = oltp for OS-level tuning.

Use Cases

Use the OLTP template for:

  • E-commerce: Order processing, inventory, user transactions
  • Social apps: User feeds, messaging, following relationships
  • Gaming backends: Player data, leaderboards, game state
  • SaaS applications: Multi-tenant business systems
  • Web apps: CRUD-intensive workloads

Workload characteristics:

item.title: E-R Model of PostgreSQL Cluster
item.description:
PGSQL organizes PostgreSQL as clusters. Each cluster is a logical group of database instances connected through primary-replica relationships.

Each cluster is an autonomous business unit with at least one primary instance. It exposes database capabilities through services.

There are four core entities in Pigsty’s PGSQL module:

  • Cluster: An autonomous PostgreSQL business unit and the top-level namespace for other entities.
  • Service: A named abstraction that exposes capabilities and routes traffic through node ports.
  • Instance: One PostgreSQL server, including its running processes and database files, on one node.
  • Node: A hardware resource that runs Linux and Systemd. It can be a physical server, VM, container, or Pod.

Two business entities, Database and Role, complete this logical model:

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL Users
item.description:
Quick Start

Pigsty manages users declaratively. First define users in the inventory. Then run bin/pgsql-user <cls> <username> to create or modify them.

pg-meta:
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary } }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_users: [{ name: dbuser_app, password: 'DBUser.App', pgbouncer: true }] # <--- Define user list here!
Script
bin/pgsql-user <cls> <username> # Create/modify <username> user on <cls> cluster
Playbook
./pgsql-user.yml -l pg-meta -e username=dbuser_app # Use playbook to create/modify user
Example
bin/pgsql-user pg-meta dbuser_app # Create/modify dbuser_app user on pg-meta cluster

For the complete user definition reference, see User Configuration. See Access Control for roles and privileges, and Authentication for credential management.

item.title: User Guide (Debian/Ubuntu)
item.description:
Introduction

This user guide is intended to be followed sequentially from beginning to end — each section depends on the last. For example, the Restore section relies on setup that is performed in the Quick Start section. Once pgBackRest is up and running then skipping around is possible but following the user guide in order is recommended the first time through.

Although the examples in this guide are targeted at Debian/Ubuntu and PostgreSQL 17, it should be fairly easy to apply the examples to any Unix distribution and PostgreSQL version. The only OS-specific commands are those to create, start, stop, and drop PostgreSQL clusters. The pgBackRest commands will be the same on any Unix system though the location of the executable may vary. While pgBackRest strives to operate consistently across versions of PostgreSQL, there are subtle differences between versions of PostgreSQL that may show up in this guide when illustrating certain examples, e.g. PostgreSQL path/file names and settings.

item.title: Archive Push Command (archive-push)
item.description:
Accepts a WAL segment from PostgreSQL and archives it in each repository defined by the indexed repo-path option (see the Repository section for information on configuring repositories). The WAL segment may be pushed immediately to the archive or stored locally depending on the value of archive-async. With multiple repositories configured, archive-push will attempt to push to as many repositories as possible.

The archive-push is intended to be configured and called by PostgreSQL. See Configure Archiving for an example.

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL Databases
item.description:
Quick Start

Pigsty manages databases declaratively. First define databases in the inventory. Then run bin/pgsql-db <cls> <dbname> to create or modify them.

pg-meta:
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary } }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_databases: [{ name: some_db }]  # <--- Define database list here!
Script
bin/pgsql-db <cls> <dbname> # Create/modify <dbname> database on <cls> cluster
Playbook
./pgsql-db.yml -l pg-meta -e dbname=some_db # Use playbook to create/modify database
Example
bin/pgsql-db pg-meta some_db # Create/modify some_db database on pg-meta cluster

For the complete database definition reference, see Database Configuration. For database access permissions, see Access Control: Database Isolation.

item.title: Environment Configuration Settings
item.description:
It is possible to override some of the configuration parameters defined in the Patroni configuration file using the system environment variables. This document lists all environment variables handled by Patroni. The values set via those variables always take precedence over the ones set in the Patroni configuration file.

Global/Universal

  • PATRONI_CONFIGURATION: it is possible to set the entire configuration for the Patroni via PATRONI_CONFIGURATION environment variable. In this case any other environment variables will not be considered!
  • PATRONI_THREAD_POOL_SIZE: size of thread pool used by Patroni to execute asynchronous tasks and communicate via REST API with other members during leader race or failsafe checks. Minimal value is 5, default value is 5.
  • PATRONI_THREAD_STACK_SIZE: specifies the stack size to be used for threads started by Patroni. Value must be aligned by 64kB. Minimal value is 64kB, default value (set by Patroni) is 512kB.
  • PATRONI_NAME: name of the node where the current instance of Patroni is running. Must be unique for the cluster.
  • PATRONI_NAMESPACE: path within the configuration store where Patroni will keep information about the cluster. Default value: “/service”
  • PATRONI_SCOPE: cluster name
  • PG_MALLOC_ARENA_MAX: custom value for MALLOC_ARENA_MAX environment variable for postmaster process. If not set, postmaster will inherit MALLOC_ARENA_MAX value.

Log

  • PATRONI_LOG_TYPE: sets the format of logs. Can be either plain or json. To use json format, you must have the jsonlogger installed. The default value is plain.
  • PATRONI_LOG_LEVEL: sets the general logging level. Default value is INFO (see the docs for Python logging)
  • PATRONI_LOG_TRACEBACK_LEVEL: sets the level where tracebacks will be visible. Default value is ERROR. Set it to DEBUG if you want to see tracebacks only if you enable PATRONI_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG.
  • PATRONI_LOG_FORMAT: sets the log formatting string. If the log type is plain, the log format should be a string. Refer to the LogRecord attributes for available attributes. If the log type is json, the log format can be a list in addition to a string. Each list item should correspond to LogRecord attributes. Be cautious that only the field name is required, and the %( and ) should be omitted. If you wish to print a log field with a different key name, use a dictionary where the dictionary key is the log field, and the value is the name of the field you want to be printed in the log. Default value is %(asctime)s %(levelname)s: %(message)s
  • PATRONI_LOG_DATEFORMAT: sets the datetime formatting string. (see the formatTime() documentation)
  • PATRONI_LOG_STATIC_FIELDS: add additional fields to the log. This option is only available when the log type is set to json. Example PATRONI_LOG_STATIC_FIELDS="{app: patroni}"
  • PATRONI_LOG_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE: Patroni is using two-step logging. Log records are written into the in-memory queue and there is a separate thread which pulls them from the queue and writes to stderr or file. The maximum size of the internal queue is limited by default by 1000 records, which is enough to keep logs for the past 1h20m.
  • PATRONI_LOG_DIR: Directory to write application logs to. The directory must exist and be writable by the user executing Patroni. If you set this env variable, the application will retain 4 25MB logs by default. You can tune those retention values with PATRONI_LOG_FILE_NUM and PATRONI_LOG_FILE_SIZE (see below).
  • PATRONI_LOG_MODE: Permissions for log files (for example, 0644). If not specified, permissions will be set based on the current umask value.
  • PATRONI_LOG_FILE_NUM: The number of application logs to retain.
  • PATRONI_LOG_FILE_SIZE: Size of patroni.log file (in bytes) that triggers a log rolling.
  • PATRONI_LOG_LOGGERS: Redefine logging level per python module. Example PATRONI_LOG_LOGGERS="{patroni.postmaster: WARNING, urllib3: DEBUG}"
  • PATRONI_LOG_DEDUPLICATE_HEARTBEAT_LOGS: If set to true, successive heartbeat logs that are identical shall not be output. Default value is false.
Warning

The time the HA loop executes at can be very valuable information in diagnosing failovers due to resource exhaustion and similar problems. When PATRONI_LOG_DEDUPLICATE_HEARTBEAT_LOGS is set to true there will be no log generated for the HA loop execution (unless the leader changes) and hence this potentially useful information will not be available from the logs.

item.title: Installation
item.description:
Install PIG with the Linux installer, a system package, or a release archive. The current version is v1.10.2. The download page lists all release files.

Script installation

On Linux, run:

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/pig | bash

In mainland China, use:

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.cc/pig | bash

The script detects the architecture, downloads the RPM or DEB package, and installs it with rpm or dpkg. Installation requires root or sudo access.

item.title: OLAP Template
item.description:
olap.yml is optimized for online analytical processing (OLAP) on CPUs with 4-128 cores. It supports large queries, high parallelism, relaxed timeouts, and aggressive vacuum.

Pair with node_tune = olap for OS-level tuning.

Use Cases

Use the OLAP template for:

  • Data warehouses: Historical data storage, multidimensional analysis
  • BI reports: Complex report queries, dashboard data sources
  • ETL processing: Data extraction, transformation, loading
  • Data analysis: Ad-hoc queries, data exploration
  • HTAP mixed workloads: Analytical replicas

Workload characteristics:

item.title: Package Alias
item.description:
Actual alias expansion is determined by roles/node_id/vars/*.yml in the source version you use.

PostgreSQL package names differ between operating systems:

  • EL systems (RHEL/Rocky/Alma/…) use formats like pgvector_18, postgis36_18
  • Debian/Ubuntu systems use formats like postgresql-18-pgvector, postgresql-18-postgis-3

Without aliases, you need different naming rules for each system. You must also include the correct PostgreSQL version in the names.

Package Alias

Use a Package Alias to specify the same component on different platforms. Pigsty converts it to the correct package names:

item.title: Usage: pgbouncer command
item.description:
Synopsis 

pgbouncer [-d][-v][-u user] <pgbouncer.ini>
pgbouncer -V|-h

On Windows, the options are:

pgbouncer.exe [-v][-u user] <pgbouncer.ini>
pgbouncer.exe -V|-h

Additional options for setting up a Windows service:

pgbouncer.exe --regservice <pgbouncer.ini>
pgbouncer.exe --unregservice <pgbouncer.ini>

Description

pgbouncer is a PostgreSQL connection pooler. Any target application can be connected to pgbouncer as if it were a PostgreSQL server, and pgbouncer will create a connection to the actual server, or it will reuse one of its existing connections.

item.title: User Guide (RHEL)
item.description:
Introduction

This user guide is intended to be followed sequentially from beginning to end — each section depends on the last. For example, the Restore section relies on setup that is performed in the Quick Start section. Once pgBackRest is up and running then skipping around is possible but following the user guide in order is recommended the first time through.

Although the examples in this guide are targeted at RHEL and PostgreSQL 14, it should be fairly easy to apply the examples to any Unix distribution and PostgreSQL version. The only OS-specific commands are those to create, start, stop, and drop PostgreSQL clusters. The pgBackRest commands will be the same on any Unix system though the location of the executable may vary. While pgBackRest strives to operate consistently across versions of PostgreSQL, there are subtle differences between versions of PostgreSQL that may show up in this guide when illustrating certain examples, e.g. PostgreSQL path/file names and settings.

item.title: Backup Command (backup)
item.description:
When multiple repositories are configured, pgBackRest will backup to the highest priority repository (e.g. repo1) unless the --repo option is specified.

pgBackRest does not have a built-in scheduler so it’s best to run it from cron or some other scheduling mechanism.

See Perform a Backup for more details and examples.

Command Options

Backup Annotation Option (--annotation)

Annotate backup with user-defined key/value pairs.

item.title: CRIT Template
item.description:
crit.yml is for transactional workloads with increased consistency and audit requirements. It forces data checksums and Patroni strict synchronous mode. It also adds connection logging and adjusts selected WAL, timeout, and parallel-query parameters.

The template increases write latency and may block writes when no synchronous replica is available. Before use, confirm consistency objectives, failure domains, client commit settings, and availability requirements.

Also evaluate node_tune: crit. You can select host tuning and database parameters independently.

item.title: E-R Model of Etcd Cluster
item.description:
The ETCD module organizes production ETCD into clusters. A cluster is a logical entity whose ETCD instances coordinate through the Raft consensus protocol.

Each cluster is an autonomous distributed key-value store with at least one ETCD instance. It provides services through client ports.

There are three core entities in Pigsty’s ETCD module:

  • Cluster: An autonomous ETCD service unit and the top-level namespace for other entities.
  • Instance: One ETCD server process on a node, participating in Raft consensus.
  • Node: An implicitly declared hardware resource that runs Linux and Systemd.

The ETCD model has no Service entities or complex Role distinctions, unlike PostgreSQL. All ETCD instances are functionally equivalent. Raft elects one Leader; the others become Followers. Non-voting Learner members are also permitted during intermediate scale-out states.

item.title: PgBouncer compilation and installation
item.description:
Building

PgBouncer can be built with either the Autoconf-based build system or the newer, still experimental, Meson build system. Autoconf is the recommended choice for production builds and packaging for now. The Meson build is expected to become the default and the Autoconf build to be removed in a future release, so testing it and reporting any issues is very welcome. Compilation depends on a few things:

item.title: Patroni HA Management
item.description:
Overview

Pigsty uses Patroni to manage PostgreSQL clusters. It handles configuration changes, status checks, switchovers, restarts, replica reinitialization, and other operations.

To manage clusters with Patroni, use one of these identities:

  • On an INFRA node, use an administration user to manage all clusters in the environment.
  • On a PGSQL node, use pg_dbsu, which defaults to postgres, to manage only the current cluster.

Patroni provides the patronictl administration CLI. Pigsty provides the pg wrapper alias to simplify its use.

item.title: Patroni REST API
item.description:
Patroni has a rich REST API, which is used by Patroni itself during the leader race, by the patronictl tool in order to perform failovers/switchovers/reinitialize/restarts/reloads, by HAProxy or any other kind of load balancer to perform HTTP health checks, and of course could also be used for monitoring. Below you will find the list of Patroni REST API endpoints.

Health check endpoints

For all health check GET requests Patroni returns a JSON document with the status of the node, along with the HTTP status code. If you don’t want or don’t need the JSON document, you might consider using the HEAD or OPTIONS method instead of GET.

item.title: User/Role
item.description:
In this document, “user” refers to a logical object within a database cluster created with CREATE USER/ROLE.

In PostgreSQL, users belong to the database cluster, rather than a specific database. Create business users before you create business databases.

Pigsty defines roles and users through two config parameters:

  • pg_default_roles: Define globally shared roles and users
  • pg_users: Define business users and roles at cluster level

The first parameter defines roles and users shared across the environment. The second defines business roles and users for one cluster. Both parameters use arrays of user definition objects. Pigsty creates users and roles in array order. Thus, a later user can belong to an earlier role.

item.title: Check Command (check)
item.description: The check command validates that pgBackRest and the archive_command setting are configured correctly for archiving and backups for the specified stanza. It will attempt to check all repositories and databases that are configured for the host on which the command is run. It detects misconfigurations, particularly in archiving, that result in incomplete backups because required WAL segments did not reach the archive. The command can be run on the PostgreSQL or repository host. The command may also be run on the standby host, however, since pg_switch_xlog()/pg_switch_wal() cannot be performed on the standby, the command will only test the repository configuration.

item.title: Configuration Reference
item.description:
Introduction

pgBackRest can be used entirely with command-line parameters but a configuration file is more practical for installations that are complex or set a lot of options. The default location for the configuration file is /etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf. If no file exists in that location then the old default of /etc/pgbackrest.conf will be checked.

The following option types are used:

String: A text string, commonly an identifier, password, etc.

item.title: Database
item.description:
In this document, “database” refers to a logical object within a database cluster created with CREATE DATABASE.

A PostgreSQL cluster can serve multiple databases at the same time. Define the required databases in the Pigsty cluster configuration.

Pigsty customizes the template1 database with default schemas, extensions, and privileges. New databases inherit these settings from template1. Use template to select another template for instant database cloning.

By default, Pigsty adds each application database to the PgBouncer connection pool with a 1:1 mapping. pg_exporter discovers application databases automatically to monitor their objects. Pigsty also registers all databases as PostgreSQL data sources in Grafana on every INFRA node for PGCAT dashboards.

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL HBA Rules
item.description:
Quick Start

Pigsty manages HBA rules declaratively. First define HBA rules in the inventory. Then run bin/pgsql-hba <cls> to refresh them.

pg-meta:
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary } }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_hba_rules: # <--- Define HBA rules here!
 - {user: dbuser_app, db: app, addr: intra, auth: pwd, title: 'app access'}
 - {user: dbuser_api, db: all, addr: world, auth: ssl, title: 'api ssl access'}
Script
bin/pgsql-hba <cls> # Refresh PostgreSQL and Pgbouncer HBA rules for cluster
bin/pgsql-hba <cls> <ip>... # Refresh HBA rules for specific instances
Playbook
./pgsql.yml -l <cls> -t pg_hba,pg_reload # Refresh PostgreSQL HBA only
./pgsql.yml -l <cls> -t pgbouncer_hba,pgbouncer_reload # Refresh Pgbouncer HBA only
./pgsql.yml -l <cls> -t pg_hba,pg_reload,pgbouncer_hba,pgbouncer_reload # Refresh both
Example
bin/pgsql-hba pg-meta # Refresh pg-meta cluster HBA rules
bin/pgsql-hba pg-meta 10.10.10.10 # Refresh specific instance only
bin/pgsql-hba pg-meta 10.10.10.11 10.10.10.12 # Refresh multiple instances

For rule syntax, see HBA Configuration. For authentication methods, default boundaries, and credential management, see Authentication.

item.title: MINIO Cluster Model
item.description:
MINIO is the compatibility module name for object storage. Pigsty v4.5.0 deploys Silo with minio_type: silo. It groups object storage instances into a cluster.

Each cluster is an autonomous S3-compatible object store with at least one instance. It exposes services through the S3 API port.

There are three core entities in Pigsty’s MINIO module:

  • Cluster: An autonomous object storage service unit and the top-level namespace for other entities.
  • Instance: One Silo server process on a node, managing local disks.
  • Node: An implicitly declared hardware resource that runs Linux and Systemd.

Silo also retains the Storage Pool concept for expansion.

item.title: patronictl
item.description:
Patroni has a command-line interface named patronictl, which is used basically to interact with Patroni’s REST API and with the DCS. It is intended to make it easier to perform operations in the cluster, and can easily be used by humans or scripts.

Configuration

patronictl uses 3 sections of the configuration:

  • ctl: how to authenticate against the Patroni REST API, and how to validate the server identity. Refer to ctl settings for more details;
  • restapi: how to authenticate against the Patroni REST API, and how to validate the server identity. Only used if ctl configuration is not enough. patronictl is mainly interested in restapi.authentication section (in case ctl.authentication is missing) and restapi.cafile setting (in case ctl.cacert is missing). Refer to REST API settings for more details;
  • DCS (e.g. etcd): how to contact and authenticate against the DCS used by Patroni.

Those configuration options can come either from environment variables or from a configuration file. Look for the above sections in Environment Configuration Settings or YAML Configuration Settings to understand how you can set the options for them through environment variables or through a configuration file.

item.title: Pgbouncer Connection Pooling
item.description:
Overview

Pigsty uses Pgbouncer for PostgreSQL connection pooling. By default, it listens on port 6432 and proxies connections to local PostgreSQL on port 5432.

This component is optional. If you do not need many connections, transaction pooling, or query metrics, you can disable it. You can also connect directly to the database or leave Pgbouncer unused.

User & Database Management

Pigsty automatically manages Pgbouncer users and databases. When you create databases or users, it applies the database configuration and user configuration.

item.title: TINY Template
item.description:
tiny.yml is optimized for micro instances and environments with limited resources. It is designed for CPUs with 1-3 cores. It minimizes resource use, limits memory allocation, and disables parallel queries.

Pair with node_tune = tiny for OS-level tuning.

Use Cases

Use the TINY template for:

  • Dev/test: Local development, CI/CD testing
  • Low-spec VMs: 1-2 core CPU, 1-4GB RAM cloud instances
  • Edge computing: Raspberry Pi, embedded devices
  • Demos: Quick Pigsty experience
  • Personal projects: Resource-limited blogs, small apps

Resource constraints:

item.title: Expire Command (expire)
item.description: pgBackRest does full backup rotation based on the retention type which can be a count or a time period. When a count is specified, then expiration is not concerned with when the backups were created but with how many must be retained. Differential backups are count-based but will always be expired when the full backup they depend on is expired. Incremental backups are not expired by retention independently — they are always expired with their related full or differential backup. See sections Full Backup Retention and Differential Backup Retention for details and examples.

item.title: HBA Rules
item.description:
Overview

HBA (Host-Based Authentication) controls who can connect to a database, from which source, and with which authentication method. For the authentication model and default rules, see Authentication. Pigsty manages HBA rules through pg_default_hba_rules and pg_hba_rules.

Pigsty generates these files during cluster initialization or HBA refresh:

Config File Path Description
PostgreSQL HBA /pg/data/pg_hba.conf PostgreSQL server HBA rules
PgBouncer HBA /etc/pgbouncer/pgb_hba.conf Connection pool HBA rules

HBA rules are controlled by these parameters:

item.title: E-R Model of Redis Cluster
item.description:
The Redis module organizes production Redis into clusters. A cluster is a logical entity with Redis instances on one or more nodes.

Each cluster is an autonomous, high-performance cache or storage unit with at least one Redis instance. It exposes services through ports.

There are three core entities in Pigsty’s Redis module:

  • Cluster: An autonomous Redis service unit and the top-level namespace for other entities.
  • Instance: One Redis server process using a specific port on a node.
  • Node: An implicitly declared hardware resource that runs Linux and Systemd. It can host multiple Redis instances.

Redis usually runs multiple instances per node, unlike PostgreSQL. This uses multiple CPU cores on a physical server or VM. Nodes and instances therefore have a 1:N relationship. For production, Redis instances with more than 12 GB of memory are generally discouraged.

item.title: Release Notes
item.description:
Introduction

pgBackRest release numbers consist of three parts: major, minor, and patch. A major release may break compatibility with the prior major release, but v2 releases are fully compatible with v1 repositories and will accept all v1 options. Minor releases can include bug fixes and features but do not change the repository format and strive to avoid changing options and naming. Patch releases contain bug fixes for the most recent minor release.

item.title: Replica imaging and bootstrap
item.description:
Patroni allows customizing creation of a new replica. It also supports defining what happens when the new empty cluster is being bootstrapped. The distinction between two is well defined: Patroni creates replicas only if the initialize key is present in DCS for the cluster. If there is no initialize key - Patroni calls bootstrap exclusively on the first node that takes the initialize key lock.

Bootstrap

PostgreSQL provides initdb command to initialize a new cluster and Patroni calls it by default. In certain cases, particularly when creating a new cluster as a copy of an existing one, it is necessary to replace a built-in method with custom actions. Patroni supports executing user-defined scripts to bootstrap new clusters, supplying some required arguments to them, i.e. the name of the cluster and the path to the data directory. This is configured in the bootstrap section of the Patroni configuration. For example:

item.title: Access Control
item.description:
Access control combines roles, object privileges, database ACLs, and HBA. This page describes configuration parameters. For design and boundaries, see Access Control Concepts.

Pigsty provides a compact ACL model described by these parameters:

  • pg_default_roles: system roles and system users.
  • pg_users: application users and roles.
  • pg_default_privileges: default privileges on objects created by managed administrators and owners.
  • pg_revoke_public, pg_default_schemas, and pg_default_extensions: default behavior for template1.

Manage these parameters together with HBA and database definitions to produce reproducible access-control configuration.

item.title: Changelog
item.description:
PgBouncer 1.26.x

2026-10-14 - PgBouncer 1.26.1 - “Only startup once”

  • Security
    • Fix CVE-2026-107350: PgBouncer 1.17.0 through 1.26.0 processed a second StartupMessage sent during SCRAM authentication when the client connected to a non-existent database. An attacker knowing the password of a user listed in auth_file could use this to log in as any other user that authenticates using SCRAM, including admins and backend superusers. This requires SCRAM authentication to be used for both users. The impersonated user can come from either auth_file or auth_query.
    • Fix CVE-2026-107349: An unauthenticated client could make PgBouncer 1.20.0 through 1.26.0 spin forever on a CPU core, and thus stop serving all clients, by sending a startup options parameter containing an empty option name such as -c=. This is only exploitable when ignore_startup_parameters is non-empty but does not contain options.
    • Fix CVE-2026-107348: An integer overflow in the packet buffer growth logic of PgBouncer 1.21.0 through 1.26.0 could cause PgBouncer to hang in an infinite loop when a client sent a packet header declaring a length above 2^31. This is only exploitable when max_packet_size is set to 2147483649 or higher, the default of 2147483647 is not affected. Since 1.23.0 this is reachable before authentication. This is the same class of bug as CVE-2026-6668, but in a different buffer implementation.
  • Fixes
    • Make ignore_startup_parameters take precedence over tracked parameters. Since 1.26.0 search_path is tracked by default, which caused ignore_startup_parameters = search_path to silently have no effect anymore. Since the release various bugs were reported around tracking of search_path parameter. These bugs will be addressed in a later release. Adding search_path to ignore_startup_parameters now restores the 1.25 behaviour of ignoring it. (bug introduced in 1.26.0)

2026-09-23 - PgBouncer 1.26.0 - “Ignore all previous search_path”

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL Component Services
item.description:
Overview

The Pigsty PGSQL module has multiple components. Each component runs as a systemd service on nodes, except pgBackRest.

To maintain production PostgreSQL clusters, learn how these components work and how to manage them.

Component Port Service Name Description
Patroni 8008 patroni HA manager, manages PostgreSQL lifecycle
PostgreSQL 5432 postgres Placeholder service, not used, for emergency
Pgbouncer 6432 pgbouncer Connection pooling middleware, traffic entry
PgBackRest - - pgBackRest has no daemon service
HAProxy 543x haproxy Load balancer, exposes database services
pg_exporter 9630 pg_exporter PostgreSQL metrics exporter
pgbouncer_exporter 9631 pgbouncer_exporter Pgbouncer metrics exporter
vip-manager - vip-manager Optional, manages L2 VIP address floating
Important

Do not manage the PostgreSQL service directly with systemctl. Patroni manages PostgreSQL. Use patronictl commands. Direct PostgreSQL operations can make Patroni state inconsistent and trigger an unexpected failover. Use the postgres service only for emergencies when Patroni fails.

item.title: Frequently Asked Questions
item.description:
Introduction

Frequently Asked Questions are intended to provide details for specific questions that may or may not be covered in the User Guide, Configuration, or Command reference. If you are unable to find details for your specific issue here, remember that the pgBackRest Issues List in GitHub is also a valuable resource.

What if I get the “could not find WAL segment” error?

The cause of this error can be a result of many different issues, some of which may be:

item.title: Help Command (help)
item.description: Three levels of help are provided. If no command is specified then general help will be displayed. If a command is specified (e.g. pgbackrest help backup) then a full description of the command will be displayed along with a list of valid options. If an option is specified in addition to a command (e.g. pgbackrest help backup type) then a full description of the option as it applies to the command will be displayed.

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
You can set PostgreSQL parameters at several levels with different scopes and priorities. Pigsty supports four levels, from global to local:

Level Scope Configuration Method Storage Location
Cluster All instances in cluster Patroni DCS / Tuning Templates etcd + postgresql.conf
Instance Single PG instance pg_parameters / ALTER SYSTEM postgresql.auto.conf
Database All sessions in a DB pg_databases[].parameters pg_db_role_setting
User All sessions of a user pg_users[].parameters pg_db_role_setting

Priority from low to high: Cluster < Instance < Database < User < Session (SET command). Higher priority settings override lower ones.

item.title: Replication modes
item.description:
Patroni uses PostgreSQL streaming replication. For more information about streaming replication, see the Postgres documentation. By default Patroni configures PostgreSQL for asynchronous replication. Choosing your replication schema is dependent on your business considerations. Investigate both async and sync replication, as well as other HA solutions, to determine which solution is best for you.

Asynchronous mode durability

In asynchronous mode the cluster is allowed to lose some committed transactions to ensure availability. When the primary server fails or becomes unavailable for any other reason Patroni will automatically promote a sufficiently healthy standby to primary. Any transactions that have not been replicated to that standby remain in a “forked timeline” on the primary, and are effectively unrecoverable1.

item.description:
Tutorials

  • How to Set Up PgBouncer for Postgres Plus Standard Server

    Good overview of PgBouncer concepts.

Support

item.title: Manage PostgreSQL Cron Jobs
item.description:
Pigsty uses crontab to schedule routine backups, transaction freezing, and reorganization of bloated tables and indexes.

Quick Reference

Operation Quick Command Description
Configure Cron Jobs ./pgsql.yml -t pg_crontab -l <cls> Apply pg_crontab config
View Cron Jobs crontab -l View as postgres user
Physical Backup pg-backup [full|diff|incr] Execute backup with pgBackRest
Transaction Freeze pg-vacuum [database...] Freeze aging transactions, prevent XID wraparound
Bloat Maintenance pg-repack [database...] Online reorganize bloated tables and indexes

For other management tasks, see: Backup Management, Monitoring System, HA Management.

item.title: Info Command (info)
item.description:
The info command operates on a single stanza or all stanzas. Text output is the default and gives a human-readable summary of backups for the stanza(s) requested. This format is subject to change with any release.

For machine-readable output use --output=json. The JSON output contains far more information than the text output and is kept stable unless a bug is found.

To speed up execution, limit the output to only progress information by specifying --detail-level=progress. Note that this skips all checks except for availability of the stanza.

item.title: Project Metrics
item.description:
Code Coverage

pgBackRest aims to have complete function/branch/line coverage for the core C code in /src.

Function/line coverage is complete with no exceptions.

Branch coverage excludes branches inside macros and assert() calls. Macros have their own unit tests so they do not need to be tested everywhere they appear. Asserts are not expected to have complete branch coverage since they test cases that should always be true.

item.title: Standby cluster
item.description:
Patroni also supports running cascading replication to a remote datacenter (region) using a feature that is called “standby cluster”. This type of clusters has:

  • “standby leader”, that behaves pretty much like a regular cluster leader, except it replicates from a remote node.
  • cascade replicas, that are replicating from standby leader.

Standby leader holds and updates a leader lock in DCS. If the leader lock expires, cascade replicas will perform an election to choose another leader from the standbys.

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL Extensions
item.description:
Quick Start

Pigsty provides 600 extensions. To use an extension, complete four steps: download, install, configure, and enable.

pg-meta:
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary } }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_extensions: [ postgis, timescaledb, pgvector ]  # <--- Install extension packages
 pg_libs: 'timescaledb, pg_stat_statements, auto_explain' # <--- Configure preload extensions
 pg_databases:
 - name: meta
 extensions: [ postgis, timescaledb, vector ]  # <--- Enable in database
Script
bin/pgsql-ext <cls> # Install extensions defined in config on <cls> cluster
bin/pgsql-ext <cls> [ext...] # Install extensions specified on command line
Playbook
./pgsql.yml -l pg-meta -t pg_ext # Use playbook to install extensions
Example
bin/pgsql-ext pg-meta # Install defined extensions on pg-meta cluster
bin/pgsql-ext pg-meta pg_duckdb pg_mooncake # Install specified extensions

For complete extension reference, see Extensions. For available extensions, see Extension Catalog.

item.title: Frequently Asked Questions
item.description:
How to connect to PgBouncer?

PgBouncer acts as a Postgres server, so simply point your client to the PgBouncer port.

How to load-balance queries between several servers?

PgBouncer supports a comma-separated list of hosts in a database connection string. With load_balance_hosts=round-robin, new server connections rotate through that list. For example:

[databases]
app = host=pg1,pg2 port=5432 dbname=app load_balance_hosts=round-robin

You can also use external tools:

item.title: Repository Get Command (repo-get)
item.description:
Similar to the unix cat command but works on any supported repository type. This command requires a fully qualified file name and is primarily for administration, investigation, and testing. It is not a required part of a normal pgBackRest setup.

If the repository is encrypted then repo-get will automatically decrypt the file. Files are not automatically decompressed but the output can be piped through the appropriate decompression command, e.g. gzip -d.

item.title: Upgrading PostgreSQL Major/Minor Versions
item.description:
Quick Start

PostgreSQL has two types of version upgrade: minor and major. Their risk and complexity differ substantially.

Type Example Downtime Data Compatibility Risk
Minor upgrade 17.2 → 17.3 Seconds (rolling) Fully compatible Low
Major upgrade 17 → 18 Minutes Requires data dir upgrade Medium
Minor
# Rolling upgrade: replicas first, then primary
ansible <cls> -b -a 'yum upgrade -y postgresql17*'
pg restart --role replica --force <cls>
pg switchover <cls>
pg restart <cls> <old-primary> --force
Major
# Recommended: Logical replication migration
bin/pgsql-add pg-new # Create new version cluster
# Configure logical replication to sync data...
# Switch traffic to new cluster
Extension
ansible <cls> -b -a 'yum upgrade -y postgis36_17*'
psql -c 'ALTER EXTENSION postgis UPDATE;'

For detailed online migration process, see Online Migration documentation.

item.title: Watchdog support
item.description: Having multiple PostgreSQL servers running as primary can result in transactions lost due to diverging timelines. This situation is also called a split-brain problem. To avoid split-brain Patroni needs to ensure PostgreSQL will not accept any transaction commits after leader key expires in the DCS. Under normal circumstances Patroni will try to achieve this by stopping PostgreSQL when leader lock update fails for any reason. However, this may fail to happen due to various reasons:

item.title: Pause/Resume mode for the cluster
item.description:
The goal

Under certain circumstances Patroni needs to temporarily step down from managing the cluster, while still retaining the cluster state in DCS. Possible use cases are uncommon activities on the cluster, such as major version upgrades or corruption recovery. During those activities nodes are often started and stopped for reasons unknown to Patroni, some nodes can be even temporarily promoted, violating the assumption of running only one primary. Therefore, Patroni needs to be able to “detach” from the running cluster, implementing an equivalent of the maintenance mode in Pacemaker.

item.title: pig
item.description:
pig manages PostgreSQL packages, local database services, and Pigsty deployments. Choose a command below for your task. Use pig COMMAND --help to see the options supported by your installed program.

  • pig repo: manage software repositories
  • pig ext: manage PostgreSQL extensions
  • pig build: build extensions from source
  • pig install: install packages with the native package manager and translate PostgreSQL aliases
  • pig sty: manage Pigsty installation and Grafana dashboards
  • pig inventory: inspect, edit, validate, and exchange the Pigsty inventory
  • pig do: run Pigsty administration playbook tasks
  • pig pe: access pg_exporter metrics and configuration
  • pig pg: manage local PostgreSQL servers
  • pig pt: run patronictl transparently with service and config helpers
  • pig pb: manage pgBackRest backup and restore
  • pig pitr: run the full PITR workflow
  • pig context: output an environment context snapshot for humans and agents
  • pig license: issue and verify Pigsty licenses
  • pig status / update / version: inspect environment status, upgrade pig, and print version information

Global options

Option Purpose
-h, --help Show help
-H, --home PATH Select the Pigsty installation directory
-i, --inventory PATH Select the inventory
-o, --output FORMAT Output format: text (default), json, yaml, or json-pretty
--debug Enable debug logging
--log-level LEVEL Log level: debug, info (default), warn, error, fatal, or panic
--log-path PATH Write logs to a file; the default is the terminal

PIG-owned results support structured output. Raw-content commands such as inventory show and passthrough commands such as pt list retain their native output. See the command reference for details.

item.title: Repository List Command (repo-ls)
item.description:
Similar to the unix ls command but works on any supported repository type. This command accepts a path, absolute or relative to the repository path defined by the --repo-path option, and is primarily for administration, investigation, and testing. It is not a required part of a normal pgBackRest setup.

The default text output prints one file name per line. JSON output is available by specifying --output=json.

If more than one repository is configured, the command will default to the highest priority repository (e.g. repo1) unless the --repo option is specified.

item.title: Usage
item.description:
Pigsty provides three pieces of infrastructure to help users harness the collaborative superpowers of the PostgreSQL extension ecosystem:

  • Packaged Extension Catalog: Browse detailed information, usage, metadata, download links and docs for 600 packaged extensions
  • Extension Repository: Get pre-built RPM/DEB binary packages, available on 16 Linux system and architecture combinations
  • Package Manager: Use the pig CLI tool to abstract away OS and architecture differences for one-click extension installation

The full PGEXT.CLOUD directory lists 2,622 extensions, including these 600 packaged extensions. Package availability depends on the operating system, architecture, and PostgreSQL version.

item.title: DCS Failsafe Mode
item.description:
The problem

Patroni is heavily relying on Distributed Configuration Store (DCS) to solve the task of leader elections and detect network partitioning. That is, the node is allowed to run Postgres as the primary only if it can update the leader lock in DCS. In case the update of the leader lock fails, Postgres is immediately demoted and started as read-only. Depending on which DCS is used, the chances of hitting the “problem” differ. For example, with Etcd which is only used for Patroni, chances are close to zero, while with K8s API (backed by Etcd) it could be observed more frequently.

item.title: pig repo
item.description:
pig repo manages Linux package repositories. Use it to add or remove APT/YUM/DNF sources, refresh indexes, and create or extract offline bundles. repo create also supports macOS through SOW.

Command Description Notes
repo list Print available repositories and modules
repo info Show repository details
repo status Show current repository status
repo add Add repositories Requires sudo or root
repo set Clear, overwrite, and update repositories Requires sudo or root
repo rm Remove repositories Requires sudo or root
repo update Update repository cache Requires sudo or root
repo create Create local YUM/APT repository Linux: sudo/root; macOS: current user
repo cache Create offline package from local repo Requires sudo or root
repo boot Bootstrap repository from offline package Requires sudo or root
repo reload Refresh repository catalog

item.title: Restore Command (restore)
item.description: The restore command automatically defaults to selecting the latest backup from the first repository where backups exist (see Quick Start - Restore a Backup). The order in which the repositories are checked is dictated by the pgbackrest.conf (e.g. repo1 will be checked before repo2). To select from a specific repository, the --repo option can be passed (e.g. --repo=1). The --set option can be passed if a backup other than the latest is desired.

item.title: pig ext
item.description:
pig ext searches the extension catalog and installs, updates, or removes PostgreSQL extension packages on the host. It also supports PostgreSQL server packages. After installing a package, apply the SQL and configuration required by the extension.

Command Description Notes
ext list Search extensions
ext info Show extension details
ext avail Show extension availability matrix
ext status Show host-visible extension files/packages Does not query every database
ext scan Scan installed control/library files Does not query every database
ext add Install extensions Requires sudo or root
ext rm Remove extensions Requires sudo or root
ext update Update extensions Requires sudo or root
ext import Download extensions for offline use Requires sudo or root
ext link Link a PG version into PATH Requires sudo or root
ext reload Refresh extension catalog

Quick Start

This example uses a running PostgreSQL 18 instance. To install and start one, follow Getting Started.

item.title: Server Command (server)
item.description:
The pgBackRest server allows access to remote hosts without using the SSH protocol.

Command Options

TLS Server Address Option (--tls-server-address)

TLS server address.

IP address the server will listen on for client requests.

default: localhost
example: --tls-server-address=*

TLS Server Authorized Clients Option (--tls-server-auth)

TLS server authorized clients.

Clients are authorized on the server by verifying their certificate and checking their certificate CN (Common Name) against a list on the server configured with the tls-server-auth option.

item.title: Using Patroni with Kubernetes
item.description: Patroni can use Kubernetes objects in order to store the state of the cluster and manage the leader key. That makes it capable of operating Postgres in Kubernetes environment without any consistency store, namely, one doesn’t need to run an extra Etcd deployment. There are two different types of Kubernetes objects Patroni can use to store the leader and the configuration keys, the object type is selected with the kubernetes.use_endpoints configuration option or the PATRONI_KUBERNETES_USE_ENDPOINTS environment variable.

item.title: Roadmap
item.description:
Release Strategy

Pigsty uses semantic versioning: <major>.<minor>.<patch>. Alpha/Beta/RC versions will have suffixes like -a1, -b1, -c1 appended to the version number.

Major versions introduce incompatible foundational changes and major features. Minor versions usually add features and small API changes. Patch versions provide bug fixes and package updates.

Pigsty plans one major release per year and usually 4-6 minor releases. Minor releases generally follow PostgreSQL minor releases within one month. See Release Notes for the full history.

item.title: Citus support
item.description:
Patroni makes it extremely simple to deploy Multi-Node Citus clusters.

TL;DR

There are only a few simple rules you need to follow:

  1. Citus database extension to PostgreSQL must be available on all nodes. Absolute minimum supported Citus version is 10.0, but, to take all benefits from transparent switchovers and restarts of workers we recommend using at least Citus 11.2.
  2. Cluster name (scope) must be the same for all Citus nodes!
  3. Superuser credentials must be the same on coordinator and all worker nodes, and pg_hba.conf should allow superuser access between all nodes.
  4. REST API access should be allowed from worker nodes to the coordinator. E.g., credentials should be the same and if configured, client certificates from worker nodes must be accepted by the coordinator.
  5. Add the following section to the patroni.yaml:
citus:
 group: X  # 0 for coordinator and 1, 2, 3, etc for workers
 database: citus  # must be the same on all nodes

After that you just need to start Patroni and it will handle the rest:

item.title: pig build
item.description:
pig build downloads sources, installs dependencies, and produces RPM/DEB packages using Pigsty build recipes. Use it on an EL, Debian, or Ubuntu build host. Rust, pgrx, and the Xray client also support their respective macOS workflows.

Command Description Notes
build spec Initialize build specification directory
build repo Initialize required repositories Requires sudo or root
build tool Initialize build tools Requires sudo or root
build rust Install Rust toolchain Current user
build pgrx Install and initialize pgrx Current user
build proxy Set up Xray clients and servers Linux: root; macOS client: regular user
build get Download source tarballs
build dep Install extension build dependencies Requires sudo or root
build ext Build extension packages Current user
build pkg Complete pipeline: get, dep, ext Requires sudo or root

Quick Start

If the build host needs package repositories, run pig build repo. This backs up and replaces existing repository definitions. Skip this step if suitable repositories are already configured.

item.title: Privacy Policy
item.description:
Pigsty Software

For offline installation in a network-isolated environment, we receive no data about you.

During online installation, our servers or cloud provider servers log the requesting machine’s IP address and/or hostname and downloaded package names.

We will not share this information with other organizations unless required by law.

Pigsty’s primary domain is: pigsty.io. For mainland China, please use the registered mirror site pigsty.cc.

Pigsty Website

When you visit our website, our servers will automatically log your IP address and/or hostname in Nginx logs.

item.title: Server Ping Command (server-ping)
item.description:
Ping a pgBackRest TLS server to ensure it is accepting connections. This serves as an aliveness check only since no authentication is attempted.

If no host is specified on the command-line then the tls-server-host option will be used.

Command Options

TLS Server Address Option (--tls-server-address)

TLS server address.

IP address the server will listen on for client requests.

default: localhost
example: --tls-server-address=*

TLS Server Port Option (--tls-server-port)

TLS server port.

item.title: Convert a Standalone to a Patroni Cluster
item.description:
This section describes the process for converting a standalone PostgreSQL instance into a Patroni cluster.

To deploy a Patroni cluster without using a pre-existing PostgreSQL instance, see Running and Configuring instead.

Procedure

You can find below an overview of steps for converting an existing Postgres cluster to a Patroni managed cluster. In the steps we assume all nodes that are part of the existing cluster are currently up and running, and that you do not intend to change Postgres configuration while the migration is ongoing. The steps:

item.title: Sponsor Us
item.description:
Sponsor Us

PostgreSQL community members develop Pigsty as free and open-source software. It integrates the PostgreSQL ecosystem and promotes PostgreSQL adoption. If it helps you, consider these ways to support the project:

  • Sponsor the project financially.
  • Purchase Technical Support Services for PostgreSQL high-availability deployment and maintenance.
  • Share your Pigsty use cases and experiences through articles, talks, and videos.
  • Allow us to mention your organization in “Users of Pigsty.”
  • Recommend/refer our project and services to friends, colleagues, and clients in need.
  • Follow our WeChat Official Account and share relevant technical articles to groups and your social media.

Angel Investors

Pigsty received investment through Miracle Plus S22, formerly YC China. We thank Miracle Plus and Dr. Qi Lu for their support.

item.title: Stanza Create Command (stanza-create)
item.description:
The stanza-create command must be run after the stanza has been configured in pgbackrest.conf. If there is more than one repository configured, the stanza will be created on each. Stanzas that have already been created will be skipped so it is always safe to run stanza-create, even when a new repository has been configured.

See Create the Stanza for more information and an example.

Command Options

Online Option (--online)

Create on an online cluster.

item.title: User Cases
item.description:
Google Analytics page views and download statistics indicate approximately 100,000 Pigsty users. About half are in mainland China and half in other regions. They work in internet services, cloud computing, finance, autonomous driving, manufacturing, technology, ISV, and defense. Contact us to share your use case and logo. We offer one free consultation session in return.

Internet

Tantan: 200+ physical machines for PostgreSQL and Redis services

item.title: pig sty
item.description:
pig sty installs Pigsty, prepares the controller, generates configuration, and runs deployment playbooks. It also manages dashboards through the Grafana HTTP API.

Command Purpose
sty init Download and extract Pigsty into an installation directory
sty boot Install Ansible dependencies and prepare the controller
sty conf Generate and validate an inventory from a template
sty deploy Run the deployment playbook
sty list / sty get List or download Pigsty releases
sty grafana Manage Grafana dashboards, language, and theme; alias gf

Quick Start

Run these commands on the controller:

item.title: Stanza Delete Command (stanza-delete)
item.description:
The stanza-delete command removes data in the repository associated with a stanza.

WARNING:

Use this command with caution — it will permanently remove all backups and archives from the pgBackRest repository for the specified stanza.

To delete a stanza:

  • Shut down the PostgreSQL cluster associated with the stanza (or use –force to override).
  • Run the stop command on the host where the stanza-delete command will be run.
  • Run the stanza-delete command.

Once the command successfully completes, it is the responsibility of the user to remove the stanza from all pgBackRest configuration files and/or environment variables.

item.title: Subscription
item.description:
Pigsty combines tools from the PostgreSQL ecosystem with automated database management. It helps users use PostgreSQL, the world’s most popular database.

Pigsty resolves many PostgreSQL operational issues. Enterprise service quality also requires expert support and full coverage from the original provider. Pigsty Enterprise Edition adds these commercial services to the open-source edition. Choose services that meet your needs.

Consider a Pigsty subscription if you have any of these needs:

  • Run critical databases with strict SLA guarantees and full support coverage.
  • Get support for complex Pigsty and PostgreSQL issues.
  • Get guidance on PostgreSQL/Pigsty production practices.
  • Get expert help to interpret monitoring dashboards, identify performance bottlenecks and fault causes, and recommend actions.
  • Plan database architectures for security, disaster recovery, and compliance. Use your existing resources and business requirements.
  • Migrate other databases to PostgreSQL, or migrate and transform legacy instances.
  • Build observability systems, data dashboards, and visualization applications with Victoria/Grafana.
  • Move off the cloud to open-source RDS for PostgreSQL alternatives. Use solutions that are cloud-neutral and avoid vendor lock-in.
  • Get professional support for Redis/ETCD/Silo and extensions such as TimescaleDB/Citus.
  • Develop customized products and OEM branding with explicit commercial authorization.
  • Sell Pigsty as SaaS/PaaS/DBaaS, or provide technical services, consulting, and cloud services based on this distribution.

Subscription Plans

Pigsty offers the Open Source Edition and two subscription tiers. Choose Professional Edition or Enterprise Edition to meet your needs.

item.title: Integration with other tools
item.description:
Patroni is able to integrate with other tools in your stack. In this section you will find a list of examples, which although not an exhaustive list, might provide you with ideas on how Patroni can integrate with other tools.

Barman

Patroni delivers an application named patroni_barman which has logic to communicate with pg-backup-api, so you are able to perform Barman operations remotely.

This application currently has a couple of sub-commands: recover and config-switch.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
What is Pigsty, and what is it not?

Pigsty is a PostgreSQL distribution and a local-first, open-source RDS solution. It provides tools and operational practices for managing a DBMS. It is not itself a Database Management System (DBMS).

For comparison, a database is a car, a DBA is its driver, and RDS is a taxi service. Pigsty provides software to automate driving.

What problem does Pigsty solve?

Database operational expertise is scarce. Users can hire experts, rent managed RDS, or use Pigsty to automate database management. Pigsty helps users build efficient, high-quality local database services without a DBA, at less than 1/10 the cost of RDS.

item.title: pig inventory
item.description:
pig inventory (alias pig inv) inspects, edits, and validates the Pigsty inventory, pigsty.yml. It also checks deployment prerequisites and exchanges configuration with PostgreSQL through the experimental cmdb commands.

When you edit a fragment, PIG preserves the YAML content and formatting outside that fragment. Before saving, it parses the complete file again. If parsing fails or another process has changed the original file, PIG keeps the original and reports an error.

item.title: pig do
item.description:
pig do runs administration playbooks from the selected Pigsty directory. It uses the inventory to add clusters, create databases and users, install packages, or remove services.

Define the target configuration in the inventory first, then run the corresponding command. The commands invoke Ansible directly. This command group has no general --plan mode.

pig do pgsql-add pg-test 10.10.10.12 # add one PostgreSQL instance
pig do pgsql-rm pg-test 10.10.10.12 # remove one PostgreSQL instance
pig do pgsql-db pg-meta app # create or update a database
pig do pgsql-user pg-meta dbuser_app # create or update a user
pig do node-pkg pg-meta restic # install a package on selected nodes
pig do redis-add redis-meta # initialize a Redis cluster

Inventory selection is shared with sty deploy. PIG passes the resolved source to Ansible without interpreting it again relative to Pigsty home. Missing explicit, environment, or default sources fail before playbook execution. Existing directory and executable Inventory sources remain Ansible inputs; static Inventory commands do not execute them.

item.title: pig postgres
item.description:
pig postgres (alias pig pg) manages local PostgreSQL instances and databases. Use it to initialize or control an instance, run SQL, maintain tables, and create database copies. Use pig pt for Patroni cluster operations and pig pitr for recovery with pgBackRest.

Commands run as the PostgreSQL operating-system user, normally postgres. Install PostgreSQL first. For a new data directory, make its parent writable by that user or create an empty directory with the correct ownership before running pg init.

item.title: Security Considerations
item.description:
A Patroni cluster has two interfaces to be protected from unauthorized access: the distributed configuration storage (DCS) and the Patroni REST API.

Protecting DCS

Patroni and patronictl both store and retrieve data to/from the DCS.

Even when the DCS contains no sensitive information, it allows changing some of Patroni/Postgres configuration. Therefore the very first thing that should be protected is DCS itself.

The details of protection depend on the type of DCS used. The authentication and encryption parameters (tokens/basic-auth/client certificates) for the supported types of DCS are covered in settings.

item.title: Stanza Upgrade Command (stanza-upgrade)
item.description:
Immediately after upgrading PostgreSQL to a newer major version, the pg-path for all pgBackRest configurations must be set to the new database location and the stanza-upgrade command run. If there is more than one repository configured on the host, the stanza will be upgraded on each. If the database is offline use the --no-online option.

Command Options

Online Option (--online)

Update an online cluster.

item.title: Nodes
item.description:
A node represents hardware resources and an operating system. It can be a physical server, virtual machine, container, or pod.

A node needs a Linux OS, systemd, and standard CPU, memory, disk, and network resources.

Install modules on nodes. The installed modules determine the node type:

Type Description
Regular Node A node managed by Pigsty
ADMIN Node The node that runs Ansible to issue management commands
INFRA Node Nodes with the INFRA module installed
ETCD Node Nodes with the ETCD module for DCS
MINIO Node Nodes with the MINIO module for object storage
PGSQL Node Nodes with the PGSQL module installed
… Nodes with other modules…

In a single-node deployment, one node has all roles: regular, administration, infrastructure, ETCD, and database.

item.title: HA multi datacenter
item.description:
The high availability of a PostgreSQL cluster deployed in multiple data centers is based on replication, which can be synchronous or asynchronous (see replication modes).

In both cases, it is important to be clear about the following concepts:

  • Postgres can run as primary or standby leader only when it owns the leading key and can update the leading key.
  • You should run the odd number of etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul nodes: 3 or 5!

Synchronous Replication

To have a multi DC cluster that can automatically tolerate a zone drop, a minimum of 3 is required.

item.title: pig patroni
item.description:
pig patroni (alias pig pt) runs the installed patronictl command. Use it to inspect cluster members, change cluster configuration, and switch the primary. PIG selects the configuration file and provides local service, status, and log commands. Other commands use patronictl’s arguments, prompts, output, and exit codes.

Install Patroni and configure access to its cluster before running cluster operations. Use pig pt COMMAND --help for native command help, or pig pt -- --help for patronictl root help. Running pig pt alone shows PIG’s help.

item.title: Start Command (start)
item.description:
If the pgBackRest processes were previously stopped using the stop command then they can be started again using the start command. Note that this will not immediately start up any pgBackRest processes but they are allowed to run. See Starting and Stopping for more information and examples.

General Options

Allow Run as Root Option (--allow-root)

Allow the command to run as the root user.
